Budget Constrained Sequential Procedures for K Populations

Source: vignettes/seq-budget.Rmd
seq-budget.Rmd

The Research Question

A large organization trains new employees face to face at a central site. Two cheaper formats are proposed: one-on-one video calls, and a hybrid of recorded material followed by a shorter call. Face to face training costs far more per trainee than either alternative, because of travel and lodging. The organization will spend a fixed amount on a study and wants to know whether the average of the two alternatives is no worse than the face to face format by more than a margin that matters, or is equivalent to it within such a margin. This is the application that motivates Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025), and the same structure arises whenever several groups with unequal sampling costs are compared under a fixed budget: multisite program evaluations in education, marketing experiments across regions, surveys that compare strata.

With μ1 the mean score after face to face training and μ2 and μ3 the means after the two alternatives, the quantity of interest is the contrast (Equation 1 of the article)

ψ = −μ1 + ½ μ2 + ½ μ3

How should the budget be divided among the three groups so that ψ is estimated as precisely as possible? The answer depends on the population variances, which are unknown before the study. A fixed sample size plan has to take them from a guess or from a separate pilot study (the approach of Luh & Guo, 2016). The sequential procedure learns them from the data as the data arrive, in the purely sequential tradition surveyed by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), and it counts the pilot observations against the same budget and uses them in the analysis.

The Method

Take a contrast ψ of K population means with weights ci, the sum over the populations of ci μi. Its estimate is the same weighted sum of the sample means, and the variance of the estimate is the sum of ci2 σi2 / ni, where σi is the standard deviation of population i and ni its sample size. An observation from population i costs ai, and the total budget is A0. Theorem 1 of the article gives the sample sizes that minimize the variance when the total cost, the sum of aini, equals the budget (its Equation 12),

ni0 = A0 |ci| σi / (√ai × Σl |cl| σl √al)

and the minimized variance (Equation 13),

Vo = (Σi |ci| σi √ai)2 / A0

A group receives more observations when its scores vary more, when its weight in the contrast is larger, and when it is cheaper to sample. Minimizing the variance is what maximizes the power of the tests described below.

Because the σi are unknown, the sequential procedure replaces them with the current sample standard deviations si. Group i has met its criterion when its sample size Ni satisfies (Equation 18)

Ni ≥ A0 |ci| si / (√ai × Σl |cl| sl √al)

and sampling ends when every group has met its criterion or when the budget cannot pay for another needed observation. The functions divide the work as follows.

Step Function
Plan with assumed standard deviations seq_budget_optimal()
Choose the pilot size seq_budget_pilot()
Check the data in hand seq_budget()
Choose the group for the next observation seq_budget_next()
Decide noninferiority, superiority, inferiority, or equivalence decide_seq_budget_*()
Study the design by simulation before collecting data seq_budget_sensitivity()

A Priori Planning

The article’s own illustration (p. 430) has three groups, a cost of 30 per observation in each, and a budget of 10,000. When the products of weight and standard deviation, |ci| σi, are equal, the optimal size is the same in every group:

plan <- seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = c(-1, 0.5, 0.5),
  sigmas           = c(1, 2, 2),
  cost_per_group   = c(30, 30, 30),
  budget           = 10000
)
plan$n_per_group
#> [1] 111.1111 111.1111 111.1111
plan$minimum_variance
#> [1] 0.027

The sizes are not whole numbers, and they cannot simply be rounded up: 112 per group would cost 10,080. The article rounds to 111 per group, 333 observations in all, at a cost of 9,990. A few units of the budget go unspent whenever the unit costs do not divide what is left, and this is how the sequential procedure ends as well.

Costs are rarely equal. Suppose face to face training costs 500 per trainee (the figure the article uses), a video call 150, and the hybrid format 250, with a budget of 50,000 (again the article’s figure) and scores on a 30 point assessment whose standard deviations are thought to be about 3, 3.5, and 2.5:

weights <- c(-1, 0.5, 0.5)
costs   <- c(500, 150, 250)
budget  <- 50000

plan <- seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = weights,
  sigmas           = c(3, 3.5, 2.5),
  cost_per_group   = costs,
  budget           = budget
)
plan$n_per_group
#> [1] 61.95278 65.98070 36.50602
sum(costs * plan$n_per_group)
#> [1] 50000
sqrt(plan$minimum_variance)
#> [1] 0.4842398

The face to face group carries twice the weight of either alternative, yet it does not receive twice the observations, because each of its observations costs two to more than three times as much. The last line is the smallest standard error of the contrast estimate that this budget can buy if the assumed standard deviations are right.

The Sequential Workflow

The standard deviations above were guesses. The sequential procedure does not need them. It starts with a pilot from every group, which is paid for from the same budget. The article requires at least two observations per group and advises more, because variance estimates from very small samples are unstable (p. 431); its simulations used 10.

m_0 <- seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 10)
m_0 * sum(costs)
#> [1] 9000

The pilot costs 9,000 of the 50,000. To have data to work with, the scores are simulated here from populations whose true contrast is zero (the alternatives are exactly as effective as face to face training on average); in a study each new score would come from the next trainee.

set.seed(113)
true_means <- c(15, 15, 15)
true_sds   <- c(3, 3.5, 2.5)
new_score  <- function(g, k = 1) rnorm(k, true_means[g], true_sds[g])

scores <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)

out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
out
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 30
#>   Criterion n     : 164
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.01524134
#>   contrast          : 2.176975
#>   upper_limit       : 4.369191
#>   variance          : 1.251038
#>   current_total_n   : 30
#>   current_total_cost: 9000
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
attr(out, "n_per_group")
#> [1] 10 10 10
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
#> [1] 61 60 43
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
#> [1] 41000
seq_budget_next(out)
#> [1] 1

The weights and costs are matched to the groups by position. If they are named and the list of groups is named too, the names must agree in order; seq_budget() stops otherwise, so that, for example, weights typed in the order of the design are not applied to a list that split() has put in alphabetical order.

After the pilot every group is below its criterion, so sampling continues. seq_budget_next() names the group that should receive the next observation: by default the one furthest below its estimated optimal size, among the groups whose next observation the remaining budget can pay for. Because it never names a group that cannot be paid for, a study that follows it one observation at a time cannot overspend. The whole study is then a short loop (the helper term() pulls one row out of a check, here to record the running cost):

term <- function(check, name) check$value[check$term == name]

cost_path <- term(out, "current_total_cost")
repeat {
  out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], new_score(g))
  cost_path <- c(cost_path, term(out, "current_total_cost") + costs[g])
}
out
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 164
#>   Criterion n     : 166
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.1118478
#>   contrast          : 0.8450936
#>   upper_limit       : 1.802035
#>   variance          : 0.2383826
#>   current_total_n   : 164
#>   current_total_cost: 50000
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted)
#> 
#>   Note: Sampling has ended because the budget cannot pay for another
#>         observation: 0 of 50000 is left, and one more observation from
#>         a group still below its criterion (groups 1 and 2) costs at
#>         least 150.
attr(out, "n_per_group")
#> [1] 62 65 37
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
#> [1] 63 66 37
max(cost_path) <= budget
#> [1] TRUE
plot(seq_along(cost_path) - 1, cost_path, type = "s",
     xlab = "Observations added after the pilot",
     ylab = "Total cost so far", ylim = c(0, budget))
abline(h = budget, lty = 2)

Why Sampling Ends With Sizes Below the Criteria

Sampling has ended (is_satisfied is TRUE) although the current total sample size (164) is below the total of the criteria (166). The note under the printed check gives the reason: sampling ended because the budget could not pay for another observation that was still needed, not because every group reached its criterion. The attributes separate the two ways of ending:

attr(out, "rule_met")
#> [1] FALSE
attr(out, "budget_exhausted")
#> [1] TRUE
attr(out, "is_satisfied")
#> [1] TRUE
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
#> [1] 0

rule_met is TRUE when every group has met its criterion. budget_exhausted is TRUE when at least one group is still below its criterion and what is left of the budget cannot pay for one more observation from any such group. seq_budget_next() returns NA exactly when one of the two holds, and is_satisfied is TRUE then too, with one exception that is taken up below: a study in which the variance of some group is unusable is never reported as satisfied. seq_report() words the result for a methods section and names the ending for what it is:

seq_report(out)
#> Sample size was determined with the sequential budget constrained
#> procedure for a linear contrast of population means (Chattopadhyay,
#> Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, & Padalunkal, 2025), with a 95% confidence
#> interval and a total budget of 50,000. Sampling ended at a total sample
#> size of N = 164 because the budget could not pay for another
#> observation from a group still below its criterion sample size: 0 of
#> the 50,000 was left (the criterion sample sizes at that point came to
#> 166 in total). At that sample size the estimate of the contrast was
#> 0.845, 95% CI [-0.112, 1.802].
#> 
#> Reference
#> Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J.
#>     (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of
#>     a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods,
#>     30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Ending by the budget is the normal case, not a failure. Multiply each right hand side of Equation 18 by its unit cost and add them up: the sum is A0, whatever the standard deviations are. Judged on the current data, therefore, every group can be at or above its criterion without passing the budget only when each sample size equals its target exactly, which requires every target to be a whole number. Otherwise the procedure runs until what is left of the budget (here 0) is less than the cost of any observation still needed, just as 333 observations at 30 each leave 10 of 10,000 unspent in the article’s illustration.

Only the groups that still need observations count. At the end of this run groups 1 and 2 were still below the criterion, and a cheaper group that had already met its criterion would not have kept the study going. Conversely, when the most expensive group can no longer be paid for but a cheaper one still needs observations, the study continues with the cheaper one.

If the data handed to seq_budget() already cost more than the budget (a pilot the budget cannot pay for, or a loop that added observations without asking seq_budget_next()), the check says so in a note and sets the attribute budget_exceeded:

over <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 40000)
attr(over, "budget_exceeded")
#> [1] TRUE
writeLines(strwrap(attr(over, "notes"), width = 72))
#> The data already cost 50000, which is more than the budget of 40000, so
#> the budget constraint does not hold for this result. Raise the budget
#> or use a smaller pilot; once sampling is under way, choosing each new
#> observation with seq_budget_next() keeps the cost within the budget.

When Observations Arrive in Batches

seq_budget_next() names one group for one observation. A study that collects several observations at a time takes them from the group it names, but no more than the remaining budget pays for and no more than the group is still short of its criterion, and then checks again. The loop below does that for batches of up to 10, starting from the same pilot scores as the loop above.

batch <- 10

set.seed(113)
batched <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)
repeat {
  out_b <- seq_budget(batched, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                      budget = budget)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_b)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  affordable <- floor(attr(out_b, "remaining_budget") / costs[g])
  short <- ceiling(attr(out_b, "criterion_per_group")[g] -
                     attr(out_b, "n_per_group")[g])
  batched[[g]] <- c(batched[[g]],
                    new_score(g, min(batch, affordable, max(1, short))))
}
attr(out_b, "n_per_group")
#> [1] 66 60 32
term(out_b, "current_total_cost")
#> [1] 50000
attr(out_b, "budget_exceeded")
#> [1] FALSE

The study ends within the budget, with 66, 60, 32 observations in the three groups where the loop that checked after every observation ended with 62, 65, 37. A loop that adds a whole batch whatever the remaining budget is can overspend; the check then sets budget_exceeded, as in the example above, and the budget constraint no longer holds for its result.

When a Group Shows No Variation

With a small pilot and coarsely scored data, every observation in a group can be the same. Its sample variance is then zero, Equation 18 gives it a target of zero, and the stopping rule as printed in the article would end the sampling from that group with a variance estimate of zero. A variance of zero is not an estimate, and seq_budget() treats it as every check in the package treats an unusable variance, which is a deliberate departure from the article: the rule is reported as not met, the attribute variance_unusable is TRUE, and the printed notes say so. (The same holds when the scores of a group agree to about ten significant digits, so that whatever variance is computed is rounding error.)

ratings <- list(c(4, 4, 4), c(3, 5, 4), c(2, 4, 5))
flat <- seq_budget(ratings, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
flat
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 9
#>   Criterion n     : 250
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -1.199658
#>   contrast          : -0.1666667
#>   upper_limit       : 0.8663251
#>   variance          : 0.2777778
#>   current_total_n   : 9
#>   current_total_cost: 2700
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
#> 
#>   Note: The variance estimate is not yet usable at this sample size (it
#>         is zero, negative, or not finite), so the stopping rule is
#>         reported as not met. Collect more data and check again.
#> 
#>   Note: The observations in group 1 are all equal, or differ too little
#>         relative to their size for a variance to be computed, so its
#>         share of the budget cannot be estimated yet. seq_budget_next()
#>         names such a group when no group whose variance can be
#>         estimated has fewer observations.
attr(flat, "variance_unusable")
#> [1] TRUE
seq_budget_next(flat)
#> [1] 1

seq_budget_next() names such a group whenever no group whose variance can be used has fewer observations than it has, so the group is sampled at the pace of the least sampled of the others until its scores differ; one or two more observations usually settle it. A group that really is constant (a ceiling or a floor on the measure) keeps that pace to the end, which can take a large part of the budget when the group is expensive, and the study ends with is_satisfied still FALSE and a result that the decision functions refuse. If a group shows no variation after more than a few observations beyond the pilot, stop and reconsider the measure before spending the rest of the budget.

Hypothesis Decisions

When sampling has ended, the estimate and its standard error are used for the test the study was designed for. The four decision functions are one family. Each is a one-sided test at level alpha_level, 0.05 by default as in the article’s tables, computed from the contrast estimate and its standard error, the square root of the row variance; equivalence is two such tests. None of them reads the interval printed on the check, whose confidence level is two-sided, so the confidence level of the check does not enter a decision. Below, SE stands for that standard error and zα for the upper 100α percent point of the standard normal distribution (1.645 for α = 0.05).

The article formulates noninferiority with inferiority as the null hypothesis (its Equations 6 and 7): for a margin δ > 0 fixed in advance (the article’s |ψ0|), the null hypothesis is ψ ≤ −δ and the alternative is ψ > −δ. The null hypothesis is rejected at one-sided level α when the estimate is above −δ + zα SE (Equation C3). The formulation assumes that a larger response is better, which is why the contrast was written with the face to face format entering negatively. The margin argument is the size of the margin, a positive number. The article illustrates equivalence with a margin of 1.25 points; the same margin is used here.

decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 1.25)
#> [1] TRUE

The estimate is 0.85 with a standard error of 0.49, so the estimate minus 1.645 standard errors, the lower limit of a 90 percent interval, is 0.04, which is above −1.25: inferiority is rejected, and noninferiority is declared.

Equivalence is two one-sided tests, each at level α (Equations 11 and C15): the contrast is declared to lie between the margins ψ1 and ψ2 when the estimate is above ψ1 + zα SE and below ψ2 − zα SE. The two margins are given as they are, with their signs.

decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -1.25, margin_upper = 1.25)
#> [1] FALSE

The 90 percent interval runs from 0.04 to 1.65. Its upper limit is above 1.25, so equivalence within 1.25 points is not declared. The interval is not too wide for the margins: it is 1.61 wide, and the band between them is 2.5 wide. It crosses a margin because the estimate in this run lies 1.7 standard errors above the true contrast of zero. The scores were simulated from formats that are equally effective, so the failure to declare equivalence is a Type II error of this run and not a verdict on the budget.

How often a study on this budget declares equivalence when the formats are equally effective can be worked out before any data are collected. The test declares it when the estimate is within 1.25 − zα SE of zero. Take for SE the smallest standard error this budget allows, from the plan in the section on a priori planning, and take the estimate to be normally distributed around a true contrast of zero:

se_best <- sqrt(plan$minimum_variance)    # smallest standard error
reach <- 1.25 - qnorm(0.95) * se_best     # declared when |estimate| < reach
c(reach = reach,
  noninferiority = pnorm(reach / se_best),
  equivalence = 2 * pnorm(reach / se_best) - 1)
#>          reach noninferiority    equivalence 
#>      0.4534964      0.8254952      0.6509904

By this approximation the budget declares noninferiority in about 83 percent of studies and equivalence in about 65 percent when the true contrast is zero. Equivalence asks more of a study than noninferiority does, because the estimate has to stay clear of both margins.

The other two functions are the one-sided tests against a single margin, which is given with its sign. For a margin m, decide_seq_budget_superiority() tests the null hypothesis ψ ≤ m against the alternative ψ > m. With a positive margin it is the article’s superiority test (Equations 8 and 9), with a margin of zero it asks whether the alternatives are better than face to face training at all, and noninferiority is its special case margin = -abs(delta):

decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -abs(1.25))
#> [1] TRUE
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0)
#> [1] TRUE

The first line repeats the noninferiority decision, because a contrast above −δ and noninferiority with margin δ are the same hypothesis. The second declares the alternatives better than face to face training, because the lower limit of the 90 percent interval (0.04) is just above zero. These scores were simulated with a true contrast of zero, so this is a Type I error, which a test at level 0.05 makes in about one study in twenty when the true contrast equals the margin. It has the same cause as the failure to declare equivalence: one estimate that came out well above the true value. decide_seq_budget_inferiority() is the mirror image, the null hypothesis ψ ≥ m against the alternative ψ < m: it concludes that the contrast is below the margin, with that conclusion as the alternative hypothesis. It is not the article’s noninferiority test, in which inferiority is the null hypothesis.

decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 0)
#> [1] FALSE

These two tests are the halves of the equivalence test. In the article they are its Equations C11 to C14: equivalence between ψ1 and ψ2 is declared exactly when the superiority test at ψ1 and the inferiority test at ψ2 both reject.

decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -1.25) &&
  decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 1.25)
#> [1] FALSE

A stricter test is a smaller alpha_level. The limits that a test at level α compares with its margins are those of a check computed with conf_level = 1 - 2 * alpha_level; for the default level that is the 90 percent interval quoted above.

decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0, alpha_level = 0.025)
#> [1] FALSE

out_90 <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                     budget = budget, conf_level = 1 - 2 * 0.05)
c(term(out_90, "lower_limit"), term(out_90, "upper_limit"))
#> [1] 0.04200302 1.64818417

At one-sided level 0.025 the alternatives are no longer declared better than face to face training.

The level of each test is stated for one decision, made when sampling has ended. Asked for a decision earlier, the functions return it with a warning that it is provisional.

What to Expect Before the Study

seq_budget_sensitivity() runs the whole procedure many times for assumed means, standard deviations, costs, and budget, and reports what it delivers. Here the alternatives are taken to be exactly as effective as face to face training, so the rejection rate of the noninferiority test is its power at a true contrast of zero.

sens <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means       = true_means,
  true_sds         = true_sds,
  contrast_weights = weights,
  cost_per_group   = costs,
  budget           = budget,
  margin           = 1.25,
  G                = 400,
  seed             = 113,
  m_0              = 10
)
print(sens, digits = 4)
#> term                           value
#> true_contrast                  0
#> budget                         50000
#> conf_level                     0.95
#> replications                   400
#> coverage                       0.93
#> mean_total_cost                49910
#> sd_total_cost                  92.09
#> pct_within_budget              100
#> pct_rule_met                   0
#> mean_n_1                       61.59
#> mean_n_2                       66.38
#> mean_n_3                       36.63
#> optimal_n_1                    61.95
#> optimal_n_2                    65.98
#> optimal_n_3                    36.51
#> mean_estimated_variance        0.2319
#> mean_true_variance             0.2363
#> empirical_variance             0.2336
#> optimal_variance               0.2345
#> margin                         1.25
#> alpha_level                    0.05
#> noninferiority_rejection_rate  0.845

No replication went over the budget (pct_within_budget is 100), which holds by construction. The mean final sizes are close to the optimal ones. Three rows describe the variance of the estimator and are to be read against optimal_variance, the smallest the budget allows (0.234): the mean of the estimated variance at stopping (0.232), the mean true variance at the final sample sizes (0.236, which no allocation within the budget can push below the optimum), and the variance actually observed over the replications (0.234, the noisiest of the three). The interval covered the true contrast in 93.0 percent of the 400 replications (Monte Carlo standard error 1.3 percentage points), and with a margin of 1.25 this budget rejects inferiority in about 84.5 percent of studies when the formats are in fact equally effective (Monte Carlo standard error 1.8 percentage points), which agrees with the 83 percent that the normal approximation gave in the section on hypothesis decisions.

Two cautions. First, the interval and the tests are asymptotic. The estimated variance tends to run slightly below the true one (sample standard deviations underestimate population ones on average, and the allocation follows them). The Details of ?seq_budget_sensitivity report runs of 10,000 replications of five designs with a pilot of 10 and about 15 to 120 observations per group: coverage of the 95 percent interval was 0.936 to 0.949 for normal populations and 0.925 to 0.941 for skewed ones, and the noninferiority test, with the true contrast exactly at the margin and a nominal level of 0.05, rejected in 0.050 to 0.061 of studies for normal populations and in 0.040 to 0.085 for skewed ones. A smaller pilot makes the shortfall larger, and the minimum pilot of two makes it much larger; the help page of seq_budget_pilot() gives measured figures, and the m_0 argument of seq_budget_sensitivity() shows the effect for a design of interest. Second, the procedure makes the most of a budget; it does not promise a given power. A study that needs more must raise the budget or accept a wider margin. (The values above are shown to four significant digits; the stored values are not rounded. A reported analysis deserves more replications than the 400 used to keep this vignette quick.)

The Article’s First Passage Rule

In the article a population stops being sampled the first time it meets its criterion and is never sampled again, and the populations still open receive one observation each per stage, in decreasing order of their standard deviations (pp. 429 to 430). A check sees only the data in hand, so by default seq_budget() judges every group afresh at each check: a group that met its criterion earlier and has fallen below it again, because the other standard deviations moved, receives further observations, and the next observation always goes to the group furthest below its estimated optimal size. That default is this package’s choice, not the article’s procedure. For the article’s first passage rule, hand each check the groups that the previous check closed and ask for the article’s order:

set.seed(113)
scores_fp <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)
closed <- NULL
repeat {
  out_fp <- seq_budget(scores_fp, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                       budget = budget, closed = closed)
  closed <- attr(out_fp, "met_per_group")
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_fp, order = "rounds")
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores_fp[[g]] <- c(scores_fp[[g]], new_score(g))
}
attr(out_fp, "n_per_group")
#> [1] 61 71 33
attr(out_fp, "rule_met")
#> [1] TRUE
attr(out_fp, "remaining_budget")
#> [1] 600

Under this rule every group can have met its criterion, each at its own time, with part of the budget still unspent. (The loop is the package’s reading of the article’s sequence rather than a step for step copy: ?seq_budget_next lists three details that differ, the main one being that a check judges every open group each time, where the article judges a population only after an observation drawn from it.) The two readings can be compared for a design with the procedure argument of seq_budget_sensitivity():

sens_fp <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means, true_sds, weights, costs, budget,
  margin = 1.25, G = 400, seed = 113, m_0 = 10,
  procedure = "first_passage"
)
rows <- c("mean_total_cost", "pct_rule_met", "mean_n_1", "mean_n_2",
          "mean_n_3", "mean_true_variance", "coverage")
data.frame(
  term = rows,
  reallocate = round(sens$value[match(rows, sens$term)], 3),
  first_passage = round(sens_fp$value[match(rows, sens_fp$term)], 3)
)
#>                 term reallocate first_passage
#> 1    mean_total_cost  49909.875     49849.625
#> 2       pct_rule_met      0.000        24.750
#> 3           mean_n_1     61.587        61.748
#> 4           mean_n_2     66.382        65.598
#> 5           mean_n_3     36.635        36.545
#> 6 mean_true_variance      0.236         0.237
#> 7           coverage      0.930         0.938

Under the article’s rule about 25 percent of the studies ended with every group having met its criterion and money left over; under the default none did, and on average 60 more of the budget was spent. The two readings give intervals of practically the same quality. In the simulations reported in the Details of ?seq_budget (three designs from Table 1 of the article, each with a budget of 5,000 and a pilot of 10, for normal and for skewed populations), the default left about 10 to 12 of the budget unspent where the first passage rule left 19 to 42, the true variance of the estimator at the final sample sizes was 0.2 to 1.0 percent smaller under the default, and coverage differed by at most 0.006, in either direction. The difference in coverage in the table above (0.930 against 0.938) is within Monte Carlo error at 400 replications, where each figure has a standard error of about 0.013.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Luh, W. M., & Guo, J. H. (2016). Sample size planning for the noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast with cost considerations. Psychological Methods, 21(1), 13–34. doi:10.1037/met0000039
